question.text: How can you draw the circle of a football field?

answers.answer: Fix a point as the centre and mark points at the same distance from it all the way round.
solution: A circle is the set of points at a constant distance from a fixed point (definition-1).
Fix a peg at the centre spot of the field.
Tie a rope to the peg. Its length is the radius.
Keep the rope tight and walk round the peg, marking the ground at each step.
The marked points are all the same distance from the centre, so they form the circle.

checks.resolve_answer: Fix a peg at the centre point, tie a rope of length equal to the radius to it, and walk around keeping the rope taut, marking the ground (e.g. with lime) to trace the circle.

question.text: What is your role in minimizing the consumption of water?

answers.answer: I can save water by using only the amount I need and not wasting it.
solution: This is an open question, so there is no single fixed answer.
Close the tap while brushing teeth or washing hands.
Repair leaking taps and pipes.
Do not waste water when washing cars or watering plants.
Tell family and friends to save water too.

checks.resolve_answer: Open answer: e.g. close taps when not in use, fix leaks, use water-saving irrigation, avoid wasting water when washing, reuse water.

question.text: Which chord in the following figure is a diameter in circle M ?

answers.answer: AB
solution: A diameter is a chord that passes through the centre M.
In the figure AB passes through M, but AC does not.

checks.resolve_answer: $\overline{AB}$ (it passes through the centre M)

question.text: What are the number of diameters in any circle ?

answers.answer: Infinite (unlimited) number of diameters
solution: A diameter is a chord passing through the centre (definition-6).
Infinitely many straight lines pass through the centre.
Each of these lines gives a diameter.
So a circle has an infinite number of diameters.

checks.resolve_answer: Infinitely many diameters (every chord through the centre is a diameter).

question.text: To prove that the diameter of a circle is its largest chord in length, complete: In the triangle AMC: AM + MC > ........ ; In circle M: CM = BM (radii); Thus: AM + ...... > ...... ∴ AB > ......

answers.answer: AC; BM; AC; AC. So AM + MC > AC, AM + BM > AC, AB > AC.
solution: In triangle AMC, the sum of two sides is greater than the third side: AM + MC > AC.
CM = BM (radii), so replace MC by BM.
Thus AM + BM > AC.
AM + BM = AB because M lies on AB.
So AB > AC, and the blanks are AC, BM, AC, AC.

checks.resolve_answer: AM + MC > AC; AM + BM > AC; so AB > AC (since AM + BM = AB).

judge.reason: Same blanks: AC, BM, AC, AC.

question.text: If the radius length of a circle = r then the diameter length = .......... and the perimeter of the circle = .........., area of the circle = ..........
question.notes: Continues numbered exercise list; number 4 read from green badge.

answers.answer: diameter = 2r, perimeter = 2πr, area = πr²
solution: The diameter passes through the centre and is made of two radii, so it is r + r = 2r.
The perimeter of a circle is 2πr.
The area of a circle is πr².

checks.resolve_answer: diameter = 2r; perimeter = 2πr; area = πr²

question.text: In the previous example, prove that: NC > NA.

answers.answer: NC > NA, because NC + MC > MN and MC = MA.
solution: Draw the radius MC. In triangle NMC the sum of two sides is greater than the third side: NC + MC > MN.
MC = MA (radii).
So NC + MA > MN.
A lies on MN, so MN = MA + NA.
So NC + MA > MA + NA.
Subtract MA from both sides: NC > NA (Q.E.D.).

checks.resolve_answer: A lies between M and N, so MN = MA + NA. In triangle MNC: MC + NC > MN = MA + NA. Since MC = MA (radii), NC > NA. (Q.E.D.)

question.text: In the figures opposite: What are the line segments that are equal in length? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: Fig (2): MA = MB = MC = MD, ML = MX = MY = MZ, AB = CD, and the end parts DL = XA = BY = CZ. Fig (1): CL = ZA and BY = XA.
solution: Fig (2): the chords through M are diameters of the outer circle, so MA = MB = MC = MD (radii).
The points L, X, Y, Z are on the inner circle, so ML = MX = MY = MZ (radii).
Subtracting the inner radii from the outer radii gives the equal end parts: DL, XA, BY and CZ are all equal.
Fig (1): draw MN perpendicular to chord CA. In the larger circle NC = NA, and in the smaller circle NL = NZ (corollary).
Subtracting gives CL = ZA.
In the same way, a perpendicular from M to chord BA gives BY = XA.

checks.resolve_answer: Fig (2): the lines through M are diameters, so all radii are equal (MA = MB = MC = MD and ML = MX = MY = MZ), AB = CD and LZ = XY, and subtracting inner from outer radii gives AX = BY = CZ = DL. Fig (1): the perpendicular from M to each chord bisects both the chord of the larger circle and the chord of the smaller circle, so CL = ZA and BY = XA, and MA = MB = MC (radii).

question.text: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two parallel chords in circle M. $AB = 12$ cm, $CD = 16$ cm. Find the distance between those two chords if the radius length of circle M equals 10 cm. Are there any other answers? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: 2 cm or 14 cm. Yes, there is another answer.
solution: Draw the line through M perpendicular to both chords. It bisects each chord (rule-7).
For AB = 12: half is 6 cm. The distance from M is √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8 cm.
For CD = 16: half is 8 cm. The distance from M is √(10² − 8²) = √36 = 6 cm.
If the chords are on the same side of M, the distance between them is 8 − 6 = 2 cm.
If the chords are on opposite sides of M, the distance is 8 + 6 = 14 cm.
Both positions are possible, so the answer is 2 cm or 14 cm.

checks.resolve_answer: The distance is 2 cm (chords on the same side of the centre) since the distances from M are 8 cm (AB, half = 6) and 6 cm (CD, half = 8). Yes, another answer: 14 cm when the chords are on opposite sides of the centre (8 + 6).

judge.reason: Both give 2 cm or 14 cm, with another answer existing.

question.text: If $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two parallel chords in a circle where $AB > CD$, which chord is closer to the center of the circle? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: The longer chord AB is closer to the centre.
solution: The perpendicular from M to a chord bisects it (rule-7).
A longer chord has a longer half-chord.
The distance from M to the chord is √(r² − (half chord)²).
A longer half-chord makes this distance smaller.
So AB, the longer chord, is closer to the centre.

checks.resolve_answer: The longer chord AB is closer to the centre: with half-chord h and radius r, the distance d = $\sqrt{r^2 - h^2}$, so the larger the chord, the smaller the distance.

question.text: In the figure opposite: In circle M, $\overline{MX}\perp\overline{AB}$, $\overline{MY}\perp\overline{AC}$, $m(\angle A)=60^\circ$, $m(\angle B)=70^\circ$. Find: the measures of the angles of the triangle MXY.

solution: MX ⟂ AB and MY ⟂ AC, so X and Y are the midpoints of AB and AC.
In triangle ABC, m(∠C) = 180 - 60 - 70 = 50°.
XY ∥ BC, so m(∠AXY) = 70° and m(∠AYX) = 50°.
Check with quadrilateral AXMY: 360 - 90 - 90 - 60 = 120°.
